conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. You came in with fever, nausea, and vomiting—how are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. The nausea has calmed down since I got some medicine in the ER. But I was never having belly pain—someone must’ve written that down wrong.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks for clarifying. We saw your outside CT showed some gallbladder wall thickening, so we wanted to check if that was the cause. But your ultrasound today shows no signs of acute cholecystitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my gallbladder? I was worried I might need surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, surgery isn’t needed. The ultrasound shows your gallbladder is distended but compressible, and there’s no wall edema. It doesn’t look like active infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to hear. I’ve had enough surgeries already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We reviewed your history—you’re on warfarin for your mechanical mitral valve, and your INR came back at 6.6 today. That’s higher than we want.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s not good. My INR has been all over the place before. Should I stop my warfarin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll hold it for now. You’ll get a small dose of vitamin K to help bring it down safely. We’ll restart it once we’re sure it’s under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you. I just don’t want to have a clot or bleed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re balancing that. You’re also on dialysis—your creatinine is high, but that’s expected. We’ll schedule dialysis tomorrow to help clear some toxins.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’m usually on MWF. I’ve missed one already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve scheduled you for tomorrow at noon. That should help with your overall feeling of being unwell.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. My transplant team always says dialysis makes a big difference.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from this morning show your INR dropped to 10 after the vitamin K. Still high, but moving in the right direction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s still that high? I thought the vitamin K would work faster.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s improving. We’ll keep monitoring. Your liver enzymes were a bit elevated yesterday—AST and ALT—but they’re already coming down. That suggests a mild viral illness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So this was just a virus? That makes sense—I had a low-grade fever at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and your blood cultures show no growth, so we don’t think it’s bacterial. We stopped the antibiotics from the outside hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I don’t need more meds than necessary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How did dialysis go?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Smooth. I already feel a bit more clear-headed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your repeat labs show your kidney function improved—creatinine down to 4.5. Bicarbonate is normalizing too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my INR?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Down to 2.8 this morning—much safer. We’re going to restart your warfarin at 5 mg tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Same dose as before? I was on 2.5 mg last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re going back to 5 mg. Your transplant team was consulted—they agree. You have a history of labile INRs, so they want you on the higher dose with close monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember last time I was on 2.5 mg, my INR dropped too low. Okay, I’ll stick with 5 mg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your INR is stable at 2.8, and your liver tests are now normal. You’ve been fever-free for over 24 hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely tomorrow morning. We’ll make sure your warfarin plan is clear. You’ll need to check your INR at the lab on Monday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if it’s too low?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have Lovenox at home. If your INR is below 2.5, start it as a bridge and call the anticoagulation clinic. They’ll guide you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve done that before. I’ll call them right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. Your final labs look good—INR 2.9, kidney function stable, no signs of infection. You’re ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What about my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your home medications—tacrolimus, prednisone, sevelamer, aspirin. We added tramadol for your hand pain if the lidocaine patches aren’t enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. And I’ll keep weighing myself daily, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and call if you gain more than three pounds in a day. Follow up with your PCP and transplant team as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for taking such good care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in clinic if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—my foot ulcer. Should I get it checked?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, keep it clean and dry. See your wound care team soon. Let us know if it gets red or starts draining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’ve been avoiding it because it hurts to take the bandage off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understood. But it’s important to monitor. Maybe ask your home nurse to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good idea. I’ll call them when I get home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. All right, the discharge papers are ready. You can head out whenever you’re packed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Stay well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.
